name: Geopolitical Arms Race Loop
subject: quantum-computing
subjectTitle: A Skeptic's Guide to Quantum Computing

lesson.title: The Loop Where No One Can Afford to Blink First
lesson.summary: The geopolitical arms race loop is a reinforcing loop in which one nation's investment in quantum computing capability, driven mainly by fear of falling behind militarily or economically, triggers rival nations to increase their own investment, reinforcing the first nation's fear independent of how close any side actually is to a working machine.
lesson.body:
The hype reinforcement loop in the earlier chapter ran mainly on public attention and media coverage. The geopolitical arms race loop is a different reinforcing loop, built from the same components covered in the reinforcing feedback loop and government funding pressure chapters, but running on a different fuel: national security fear rather than public enthusiasm. It can operate at full strength even in a country where the public has never heard of quantum computing, because the actors driving it are governments and defense agencies responding to each other, not to headlines.

The loop traces cleanly through the language of the security dilemma, a well established idea in international relations. Nation A increases funding for quantum computing research, partly out of genuine interest but significantly out of concern that a rival could develop a cryptographically relevant quantum computer first. Nation B observes Nation A's increased investment and, unable to verify from the outside how close Nation A actually is, must assume the worst case and respond in kind. Nation A then observes Nation B's increase and, facing the same verification problem in reverse, funds further to stay ahead. Each side's rational response to uncertainty about the other becomes the trigger for the other side's next round of investment, and the loop reinforces itself without either side needing to be wrong about anything.

The concrete mechanism driving this today is the cryptographic threat, sometimes shorthanded as Q-day, the hypothetical date when a powerful fault-tolerant quantum computer could break the public key cryptography, RSA and elliptic curve schemes, that secures most digital communication and financial infrastructure. Because adversaries can already record encrypted traffic today and decrypt it later once a capable machine exists, a strategy called harvest now decrypt later, governments have strong incentive to fund quantum research and migrate to post-quantum standards well before anyone is certain such a machine will arrive. That asymmetry, being wrong about the threat costs far more than overinvesting against it, is precisely what keeps this reinforcing loop spinning.

This loop resists slowing more than the public hype loop, for a specific reason: within its own logic, proposing to reduce funding looks like unilateral disarmament rather than sober reassessment, making de-escalation politically costly even for officials who privately doubt the near-term threat. Because much of the activity happens inside classified programs, this loop needs no public excitement or media amplification to keep running. It sustains itself purely on institutional fear and the difficulty of verifying a rival's true progress from outside.

This structure is not unique to quantum computing. The same reinforcing loop, mutual fear driving symmetric escalation regardless of true underlying capability, describes the twentieth century nuclear arms race and describes current government competition around artificial intelligence as well. Recognizing it matters for a reason relevant to the rest of this book: the strength of the geopolitical arms race loop tells you that quantum computing funding is being driven, in significant part, by worst case reasoning about rivals rather than by an independent technical assessment of how close anyone is to a working machine. Remember that later in this section, when the mathematical and physical skeptics are introduced, since their arguments target that technical assessment, which this loop has no mechanism to perform on its own.
